articles.title: Federal officials identify 400 noncitizens registered to vote in Washington state: 'Tip of the iceberg'
articles.summary: Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd told Fox News Digital some noncitizens identified in the probe cast ballots as many as 27 times, with alleged votes dating back to 1984.
articles.body: The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced Monday that investigators have identified more than 400 noncitizens illegally registered to vote in Washington state, some of whom have cast ballots in multiple elections dating back decades. Many on the list are green card holders with legal immigration status and permanent residency, according to the U.S. attorney’s offices for the Eastern and Western districts of Washington. "We have identified over 400 noncitizens who are registered to vote and have voted in multiple elections. This is only the tip of the iceberg," Neil Floyd, acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, said in a statement. "We will continue to investigate and identify those who are committing crimes by voting illegally." DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS The move builds on the DOJ's legal action against Los Angeles County, where it has sought to set aside roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots sent to individuals whose citizenship status is in question. Immigration officials told Fox News Digital Tuesday that dozens of noncitizens have also been arrested nationwide in a major voter fraud crackdown. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Floyd said investigators identified hundreds of noncitizen voters by reviewing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) records, which showed that some people who applied for certain benefits had also voted. While some individuals voted only once or three times in past elections, Floyd said others voted as many as 27 times. In total, his office counted approximately 1,500 instances of noncitizens casting ballots. He emphasized that some noncitizens had been voting for decades, predating Washington’s transition to a vote-by-mail system. "I think the earliest moment we have is 1984," Floyd said. "It's early ‘90s, late ’80s, I believe." However, Floyd said he had not checked whether any of the individuals voted in the upcoming midterms, explaining that he did not want to "interfere with the current election." The number of potential noncitizen voters could represent only a fraction of the broader population, Floyd said, because the list includes only individuals who sought certain benefits in Washington state. NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS "If you take that population, and you expand it out to include all the people that are here illegally that we haven't had contact with, just my estimation is that it's going to be in the thousands," Floyd said. Federal officials said many green card holders were registered to vote without their knowledge through Washington’s Motor Voter program, which integrates voter registration into the state’s Department of Licensing. "We have heard from green card holders who were registered against their knowledge via the Washington Motor Voter program. Then they receive a ballot in the mail and assume they are legally registered — that simply is not the case," the notice said. According to the Washington secretary of state’s website, eligible residents are automatically registered to vote only if they provide proof of U.S. citizenship during a driver’s license or ID card registration process. The findings have prompted federal officials to identify patterns in how the voter registration process has failed, Floyd said. According to the DOJ notice, federal officials are asking Washington state to set aside ballots cast by the identified individuals until their citizenship status can otherwise be confirmed. "Washington is now on notice that noncitizens are voting. It is up to the state to take action to make sure that they are not allowing these noncitizens to vote illegally," the notice said. Officials warned that voting as a noncitizen can have serious consequences for those seeking to become U.S. citizens. Potential criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application, and some individuals could also face charges for fraudulent voter registration. On Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Fox News Digital numerous illegal aliens had also admitted to unlawfully registering to vote or casting ballots in U.S. elections. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Of the dozens of suspects arrested, at least 18 had voted in a federal election. The individuals were from a range of countries, including Mexico, Somalia, Honduras, Guyana, Cuba, Germany, Nicaragua, Venezuela, Vietnam, El Salvador, Cambodia, Guatemala, Portugal and Italy. Many also faced charges for numerous alleged crimes, including counterfeiting, fraud, kidnapping, DUI, sexual offenses, assault with a dangerous weapon, drug possession and burglary.

articles.title: Judge finds L.A.'s top federal prosecutor is unlawfully serving, bars him from two cases
articles.summary: The judge barred Bill Essayli from overseeing two prosecutions but delayed the order's effect, leaving his leadership of the L.A. office under a legal cloud.
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as Los Angeles' top federal prosecutor and ordered him disqualified from overseeing two criminal cases, rejecting the Justice Department's latest effort to preserve his authority.

Senior U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright, however, delayed the disqualifications from taking effect while he considers an anticipated government request for a stay pending appeal.

Although the order applies to two prosecutions, Seabright rejected the legal arrangement that has allowed Essayli to continue leading the office under the title of first assistant U.S. attorney. He concluded that the Justice Department had unlawfully delegated powers so sweeping that Essayli in effect occupied the U.S. attorney's position.

"In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a 'de facto' United States Attorney," Seabright wrote.

After learning about Seabright's ruling from The Times, Essayli on Tuesday afternoon said that his office expected it and that the case "will be decided by the Supreme Court." In a follow-up email, he said, "I look forward to serving in my current role until then."

H. Dean Steward, a defense attorney who filed a renewed motion in August challenging Essayli's authority, called the decision "a victory for the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution."

"The Trump administration ignored the laws governing the appointment of U.S. Attorneys and got caught in Los Angeles," he said in an emailed statement. "Trump and his Department of Justice violated the law again and again in an effort to install minions as chief federal prosecutors."

The dispute is part of a nationwide battle over the Trump administration's efforts to install its chosen prosecutors without Senate confirmation. Alina Habba stepped down as New Jersey's top federal prosecutor in December after an appeals court found her appointment unlawful. In Virginia, a judge's finding that Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed led to the dismissal of indictments against former FBI Director James Comey and New York Atty. Gen. Letitia James.

In his Tuesday ruling, Seabright declined to dismiss the indictments against defendants in the two cases that he banned Essayli from overseeing. Jaime Hector Ramirez and Tu Anh Tran had not shown the substantial prejudice required for that relief, he said in response to attorneys' requests to dismiss the indictments. His order bars Essayli from participating in or supervising their cases, including overseeing the attorneys handling them.

Seabright last year ruled that Essayli was "not lawfully serving" as acting U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, but allowed him to continue exercising authority as a special attorney and first assistant U.S. attorney.

The new decision follows a U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruling rejecting a similar arrangement for Nevada prosecutor Sigal Chattah. The appellate court ruled that the Department of Justice cannot keep an official who has not been confirmed by the Senate in charge of a U.S. attorney's office simply by giving that person a different title and the full powers of the job.

The Trump administration has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review the Nevada decision, arguing that federal law allows the attorney general to delegate a vacant office's powers and install a new first assistant as its acting leader. The Supreme Court has not said whether it will take up the case.

The Justice Department sought to address the 9th Circuit ruling through a revised delegation of authority expressly excluding certain powers reserved for a U.S. attorney. At an Oct. 13 hearing, Assistant U.S. Atty. Alexander Robbins argued before Seabright that the revised delegation placed Essayli's authority on the permissible side of the line drawn by the appeals court.

Seabright found that the revision made no meaningful difference because those powers could not have been delegated to Essayli in the first place.

"Withholding the three specific statutory powers mentioned in the revised designation order in reality withholds nothing," Seabright wrote.

A former Republican member of the California Assembly from Riverside, Essayli has used his position to act as one of Trump's fiercest legal foot soldiers. He has pursued criminal charges against protesters, activists and immigrants while dropping cases involving administration allies and supporting lawsuits challenging transgender and environmental policies in California.

Essayli was sworn in as interim U.S. attorney in April 2025. Around the time he hit that role's 120-day limit, he resigned and then-Atty. Gen. Pam Bondi appointed him as a special attorney and designated him first assistant in an attempt to make him acting U.S. attorney.

Seabright rejected that maneuver last year. But the judge initially permitted him to supervise prosecutions in his other roles — an arrangement the subsequent 9th Circuit ruling undermined.

Trump still had not nominated anyone to serve as U.S. attorney for the Central District of California as of Tuesday's ruling, Seabright noted.

At the Oct. 13 hearing, Robbins said the government would appeal any disqualification ruling and warned of "the chaotic practical effects" of an order taking effect without a stay.

Under the schedule accepted by Seabright, prosecutors have five business days after the ruling to seek a stay pending appeal. If he denies that request, the disqualifications would take effect one week later, subject to further orders from him or an appellate court.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Murkowski backs Alaska Democrat for governor
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in Alaska’s governor’s race Tuesday, crossing party lines to back the former state lawmaker over three Republican candidates. In a statement released by Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign, Murkowski praised the Democrat for his commitment to bipartisanship, arguing that Alaska needs a governor willing to work with lawmakers from both…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in Alaska’s governor’s race Tuesday, crossing party lines to back the former state lawmaker over three Republican candidates.

In a statement released by Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign, Murkowski praised the Democrat for his commitment to bipartisanship, arguing that Alaska needs a governor willing to work with lawmakers from both parties.

“Our future is too important to be hamstrung by partisan divisions,” Murkowski said. “Jonathan understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”

In an interview with Alaska News Source , Murkowski ripped outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s (R) administration for failing to take advantage of federal funding opportunities.

“I have found fault with the Dunleavy administration,” she said. I think that they have left federal money on the table. I think in certain areas, where we have worked hard to put opportunities from the federal side, here, into the state, the state has failed with it.”

Kreiss-Tomkins, who represented Sitka and surrounding communities in the state House for a decade, has campaigned on bipartisan cooperation. He pledged to include Republicans and independents in his administration if elected.

“I’m honored to have Senator Murkowski’s support,” he said in a statement. “Alaskans deserve a government that can work through disagreements and make progress on the issues that matter.”

The endorsement comes just a week before Election Day, where Kreiss-Tomkins leads a four-way race to replace the term-limited Dunleavy. A September New York Times/Siena poll found Kreiss-Tomkins leading with 40 percent support among likely voters, followed by Bernadette Wilson (R) at 20 percent, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson (R) at 15 percent and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor (R) at 11 percent.

President Trump, a critic of ranked-choice voting , endorsed Wilson earlier this month and has urged Bronson and Taylor to drop out of the race to avoid splitting the Republican vote.

Trump has repeatedly attacked Murkowski for crossing party lines, calling her the “Republicans’ Worst Senator” and a “DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country” in a recent Truth Social post.

Murkowski, who has frequently broken with her party, previously endorsed former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) in her unsuccessful 2024 reelection bid. She is backing Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in his reelection campaign against Peltola this year.

articles.title: Federal grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson
articles.summary: A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department’s attempt to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony to lawmakers about President Trump’s actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Justice Department attorney Neville Hedley told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury…
articles.body:
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department’s attempt to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony to lawmakers about President Trump’s actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

Justice Department attorney Neville Hedley told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury had not concurred on the proposed charges, though he did not specify the defendant. People familiar with the situation told The Washington Post that Hedley, who identified himself as the acting senior litigation counsel, was referring to Hutchinson.

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ for comment.

The decision marks another setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to pursue criminal charges against the president’s political adversaries.

Hutchinson, a former aide to Trump’s onetime White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, became a key witness in the House investigation into the Capitol attack. She testified in June 2022 about the president’s actions leading up to the riot.

She told lawmakers that Trump allegedly knew some of his supporters were armed when he encouraged them to march to the Capitol as Congress gathered to certify former President Biden’s 2020 election victory.

Hutchinson also testified that she had been told Trump lunged toward a Secret Service agent and attempted to grab the steering wheel of his presidential vehicle after learning he would not be taken to the Capitol.

The former aide acknowledged that she was not a witness to the incident herself, and her account was later disputed by Secret Service personnel.

Trump and his allies have repeatedly accused Hutchinson of lying to Congress during her testimony.

Earlier this year, Reps. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) and Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.) referred Hutchinson to the DOJ for potential prosecution, alleging that she provided false testimony to the congressional committee.

In an unusual move, the investigation was handled by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, led by Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon.

Some federal prosecutors had privately expressed doubts about the strength of the case against Hutchinson and whether a conviction could be secured, The New York Times reported.

Grand juries rarely reject proposed indictments because prosecutors only need to convince a majority of jurors that a crime occurred, a substantially lower standard than the proof required for a conviction.

articles.title: Trump reups calls to put Cruz on Supreme Court in vacancy scenario
articles.summary: President Trump joked Tuesday that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would be his pick for the next Supreme Court vacancy, saying the senator could get unanimously confirmed because lawmakers in both parties would jump at the chance to get rid of him in Congress. During a midterm rally in Lubbock, Texas, the president praised Cruz as…
articles.body:
President Trump joked Tuesday that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would be his pick for the next Supreme Court vacancy, saying the senator could get unanimously confirmed because lawmakers in both parties would jump at the chance to get rid of him in Congress.

During a midterm rally in Lubbock, Texas, the president praised Cruz as a “brilliant lawyer” before suggesting he had found a way around the often-contentious Supreme Court confirmation process.

“I picked three Supreme Court justices, and it’s very hard to get them approved,” Trump said, referring to his appointments of Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “I said, ‘Look, I have an answer to it.’ Ted is a brilliant guy, brilliant lawyer, brilliant all that,” he said.

Trump continued, “Went to law school, top student, everything, top credentials. I said, ‘I have an answer to not being able to get it past the Democrats or the Republicans together.’ I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice.”

Trump predicted that in an unusual move, Democrats would “100 percent” support the nomination because “they hate the guy and they want to get rid of him.”

“And the Republicans would 100 percent vote for it because they can’t stand him,” he continued. “They would like to get rid of him. So I’d get 100 percent of the vote, and he would be a Supreme Court justice, and he’d do a great job.”

The president has repeatedly floated Cruz as a potential Supreme Court pick, often using the prospect of his nomination to poke fun at the Texas Republican’s complex relationships with his Senate colleagues.

He made a similar joke earlier this year during a White House event in July promoting Trump Accounts, suggesting Cruz’s departure from the Senate would be one of the few things Democrats and Republicans could agree on.

Cruz, however, has made it clear he has no plans to trade his Senate seat for a lifetime appointment to the nation’s highest court.

At an April event hosted by The Wall Street Journal, Cruz said Trump has spoken to him “seriously” about filling a hypothetical vacancy, but said his priority is policy fights rather than legal battles.

“In the first Trump term, the president spoke to me seriously about all three vacancies, and three times I said no, because I don’t want to be out of the arena of the political battle,” Cruz said during a Wall Street Journal Opinion Live interview.

Trump is heading to San Antonio, Texas, for a campaign event in support of Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton and Rep. Carlos De La Cruz (R-Texas).

articles.title: Trump and Talarico hold dueling Texas rallies
articles.summary: President Trump and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) shared their competing visions Tuesday as the two held dueling rallies in the Lone Star State one week before the midterm elections. Trump did two rallies in Texas — the first in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock. It’s his fourth trip to Texas to support…
articles.body:
President Trump and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) shared their competing visions Tuesday as the two held dueling rallies in the Lone Star State one week before the midterm elections.

Trump did two rallies in Texas — the first in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock . It’s his fourth trip to Texas to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Talarico held his own rally in Lubbock on Tuesday. He was in Corpus Christi on Saturday.

The Texas race is one of the most contested and watched Senate races in the country. Talarico and Paxton remain close in the polls — Real Clear Polling calls the race a toss-up, with Talarico holding a slight lead.

A Democrat winning the Senate seat would be a shock — none have won a U.S. Senate race in Texas since 1988, and Trump won the state by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

Democrats are vying to take control of the House and the Senate. The party would need to win four seats to win control of the Senate.

The president started off his rally in Corpus Christi saying that Texans would defeat “Democrat Communist James Talafreako,” using the nickname he’s given to the candidate.

At both rallies, Trump criticized Talarico on a range of issues like immigration, the Second Amendment and barbecue.

“If you’re running in Texas and if you don’t like guns, and if you don’t like meat and if you don’t like oil, I think you should be losing by a lot,” Trump said at the first rally about Talarico. “Where the hell did they get this guy?”

Trump spoke heavily about the Venezuelan oil tanker that arrived in Texas on Tuesday that is carrying oil to be refined in the state. He said that Talarico would try to take it away.

“Talafreako stated that he wants to dismantle Texas oil and gas and capitalism itself. He wants to take it apart,” Trump continued, adding that Talarico will “kill millions of Texas jobs.”

In Lubbock, Trump said Talarico “wants to get rid of your guns. He wants to get rid of your oil. Wants to get rid of your meat. He can’t stand the stuff.”

Talarico has denied being vegan and said he supports the Second Amendment, but advocates for gun control.

Talarico, for his part, thanked Texans for showing up for his rally in Lubbock, just three miles away from Trump’s, invoking Trump’s nickname for him.

“That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room,” he said.

He said Texans are “ready for change” and hit the Trump administration over the Iran war and tariffs.

“Change that will roll back these corrupt tariffs that are raising grocery prices. Change that will end this corrupt war in the Middle East, driving up gas prices,” he said. “We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We’re done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new.”

The Democratic Texan hit on Paxton, calling him the “most corrupt politician in Texas.”

“Ken Paxton is everything that’s wrong with our politics,” he said. “He doesn’t serve us. He serves himself.”

“Ken has spent his entire career enriching himself and his donors. I’ve spent my career working with both parties to cut your property taxes, lower your housing costs, and capping your insulin copays,” Talarico continued. “I have a legislative record. Ken Paxton has a criminal record.”

Paxton has never been convicted of a crime, though he has faced criminal indictments, federal investigations and impeachment while serving as the state’s attorney general, but he was acquitted.

Talarico compared Paxton to “that one guy” at a Texas bar.

“He’s loud. He’s obnoxious. He makes everybody feel uncomfortable. He hears you say your name to the bartender and then adds his drink to your tab when you’re not looking,” he said. “That’s Ken Paxton. And I don’t know about y’all, but I am done picking up his tab.”

“This isn’t a partisan thing,” he continued. “Republicans know just as well as Democrats that there is no place for guys like Ken Paxton in Texas.”

articles.title: GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorses Democratic candidate in Alaska governor’s race
articles.summary: The Republican senator endorsed Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins over Trump-backed Bernadette Wilson a week before Election Day.
articles.body: Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorsed the Democratic candidate for governor in her home state of Alaska on Tuesday, snubbing GOP contenders who include a Trump-backed candidate a week out from Election Day. Murkowski, one of President Donald Trump’s more vocal critics among Senate Republicans, said she is backing Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins over Bernadette Wilson, who has Trump’s endorsement. “JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now — a freshness of energy, a commonsense guy who has a known ability to be working together,” she said in an interview on NBC affiliate KTUU of Anchorage. Murkowski said she believes the three Republican gubernatorial candidates on the ballot in Alaska, which has ranked choice voting, are too partisan. “We need a governor who’s going to work with the Legislature,” she said. “That has got to happen for the delegation to be successful back in Washington, D.C.” Kreiss-Tompkins, a former state lawmaker, told KTUU he was grateful for Murkowski’s support. “I have a lot of respect for Lisa, her integrity. I think she’s worked across the aisle in Congress, which is a quality I really admire and hope to live up to if I’m elected governor,” he said. “And I’m very grateful that she wanted to step up and be a part of the coalition that we’re building.” He added that the two of them have “had a few conversations” as his campaign has progressed, “and I think she just got to a degree where she felt she was confident in our ticket and our ability to solve problems for Alaska.” In the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Kreiss-Tomkins is competing with former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, former state Attorney General Treg Taylor and Wilson, whom Trump endorsed this month. The NBC News Decision Desk rates the governor’s race in Alaska, where Trump won in 2016, 2020 and 2024, as leaning Democratic. In her comments to KTUU, Murkowski raised concerns that Wilson wouldn’t work at any point with Democrats. Wilson was dismissive of her endorsement. “Given that Senator Lisa Murkowski abandoned Alaska values a long time ago, I am not surprised that she has endorsed ‘Just Keep Taxing’ JKT,” she said in a statement, arguing that Kreiss-Tomkins’ “allegiance lies with extreme socialists hellbent on fighting President Trump to the detriment of everyday Alaskans.” Murkowski, who isn’t up for re-election until 2028, endorsed GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his re-election bid this year. He is in a competitive race that includes a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. and Democratic candidate Mary Peltola. The Trump administration sued election officials in Alaska last week, arguing that Sullivan Jr.’s appearance on the ballot could mislead voters who intended to support Sullivan’s re-election. Murkowski criticized the move, writing on X, “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.” Trump tore into Murkowski the next day on social media, calling her the “Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far.”

articles.title: James Talarico faces off against Trump in dueling Texas rallies in election’s final days
articles.summary: Voter enthusiasm in Lubbock, a Texas city of fewer than 300,000, underscored the stakes of a close Senate race in what Democrats call their best chance in a generation.
articles.body: LUBBOCK, Texas — On the day a sitting president landed in their town for the first time in 34 years, people waited for hours in lines that stretched for blocks in this reliably red city. But this crowd on the east side of the city wasn’t waiting for President Donald Trump. They wanted to see Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. “We’re all closet Democrats,” said Dr. Tim Jones, 66, an emergency room physician, laughing and gesturing to a sea of people around him in line before Talarico’s evening rally. “There are a lot of people who are finally upset at gas prices, diesel prices, inflation, lies, the war, all of it. It’s the corruption, tearing down part of the White House to build this vanity ballroom. I mean, it’s just pathetic. So people finally are deciding, ‘We’ll get out to vote.’” Less than 3 miles away, a similar scene unfolded for Trump, who held a rally at the expansive Lubbock Memorial Civic Center as he sought to boost the Republican Senate candidate, state Attorney General Ken Paxton. In a new move, Trump brought out his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who won one of the biggest rounds of applause of everyone Trump introduced. The dueling rallies and the fount of voter enthusiasm in this city of fewer than 300,000 underscored the high stakes in a Senate race that has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars in spending and presents the biggest threat in years to the Republican Party’s grip on bright-red Texas. With just a week until the election, Talarico has held a narrow lead in polling. His trip to Republican turf is a sign he is trying to win Republican crossover votes he needs for a victory. At their rally Tuesday, Democrats urged supporters to seize a once-in-a-generation chance to flip a statewide seat after three decades of Republican control. They panned the economy, high gas prices and closures of rural hospitals. Talarico repeatedly cast Paxton as corrupt and as a Trump sycophant. He called out Elon Musk, saying the tech billionaire — who has significant business interests in Texas — is trying to buy his own personal senator after having thrown more than $150 million into Paxton’s candidacy. “We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis. But we can change that in this election, in this state, in this race,” Talarico said. “We are running against the embodiment of this corrupt system. We are running against the most corrupt politician in Texas.” Republicans, meanwhile, showcased Trump, who cast Talarico as a Second Amendment-hating, meat-loathing extremist out of touch with everyday Texans. Minutes into his speech, Trump referred to him derisively as “Talafreako.” He mentioned Talarico’s disappearance from the campaign trail earlier in the month, when he said he had the flu. Trump said he believed the reason either was a “mental problem” or he was “sick to his stomach” from eating meat. While there are far more Republicans in Texas than Democrats, Republican strategists say they view the contest as a real fight at a moment when Americans are feeling anger and dissatisfaction toward Washington. Paxton has also battled his own personal scandals, creating a drag on his numbers. And Texas Republicans are still beset by infighting after a nasty primary campaign, when Trump endorsed Paxton over Sen. John Cornyn, who had the backing of much of the party’s establishment. Paxton has leaned on Trump’s advocacy. Trump has visited Texas three times this month, holding a pair of rallies Tuesday. “Is it not awesome and amazing to be onstage with the greatest president in my lifetime?” Paxton told the crowd as Trump stood behind him and looked on. Paxton said he spent the day with Trump, starting with a campaign stop in Corpus Christi. He said that as they were arriving in Lubbock, Trump told him he doesn’t normally do two rallies for any candidate: “He said, ‘I must really like you.’” “Mr. President, I really like you, too,” Paxton said. In a potential sign that Republicans were looking to attract a greater cross-section of voters, Trump handed Rubio a speaking part at the rally, as he did earlier in the day in Corpus Christi. Rubio has generally held higher approval ratings than others in the administration, including Trump. He is also a possible candidate in the 2028 presidential election. Rubio, who had stayed clear of midterm campaign rallies until Tuesday, took the microphone and kept it brief. “Our enemies are weaker. Our country is stronger, and our people are safer because Donald J. Trump is the president of the United States,” he said at the Lubbock rally. Trump called Talarico an “anti-gun extremist” and said he and Paxton are the only things standing between Talarico’s becoming a senator. “They’ve got a lot of bad people,” Trump said of Democrats. “That’s why we can’t afford to lose to some freak.” But Talarico has embraced the moniker, calling out that he had never seen so many “Talafreakos” packed into one room. “Lubbock is ready for change,” he declared to deafening screams. More than 4,000 people signed up to attend the event Tuesday night, according to his campaign. “They are scared. They are terrified. They see what we see — that we’re about to win this election.”

images.caption: James Talarico; Donald Trump
Trump gave out hats at his rally in Lubbock on Tuesday. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty
Democrats hope Talarico can help them win a Senate seat that has been in Republican control for decades. Kaylee Greenlee / Reuters

articles.title: Federal judge rules Bill Essayli unlawfully serving as de facto US attorney in California
articles.summary: Bill Essayli says the Supreme Court will ultimately decide his fate after a federal judge ruled he is unlawfully serving as a de facto U.S. attorney.
articles.body: A federal judge has disqualified Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Southern California, from overseeing two criminal cases after finding that he is unlawfully serving as a "de facto" U.S. attorney. U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright ruled Tuesday that Essayli cannot participate in or supervise the prosecutions in the two criminal cases. However, the disqualification will not take effect immediately, giving the Justice Department time to seek a stay pending appeal. "We respectfully disagree with the court's order," Essayli said in a statement provided to Fox News. APPEALS COURT RULES TRUMP ADMIN UNLAWFULLY APPOINTED NEVADA'S TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR "The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department," Essayli continued, adding that "ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then." Essayli originally served as interim U.S. attorney under an appointment that expired after 120 days. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi subsequently appointed him as a special attorney and designated him first assistant U.S. attorney. He was never formally nominated by the president or confirmed by the U.S. Senate. Seabright previously found that the arrangement did not lawfully make Essayli acting U.S. attorney but allowed him to continue supervising prosecutions under his other titles. BLANCHE SURVIVES REPUBLICAN DEFECTORS AS TRUMP GETS HIS NEW ATTORNEY GENERAL However, after the Ninth Circuit ruled over the summer against a similar arrangement involving a federal prosecutor in Nevada, Seabright decided to revisit the issue, according to the Los Angeles Times. Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a revised designation last month to narrow Essayli's authority and distinguish his situation from the Nevada case, but Seabright ruled the modified arrangement still gave Essayli enough authority to effectively occupy the vacant U.S. attorney position. "In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a 'de facto' United States Attorney," Seabright wrote. The ruling came as Essayli has been helping lead a high-profile Justice Department effort challenging California over more than 20,000 registered voters the administration says are likely noncitizens. NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS The Justice Department has asked a federal court to require ballots associated with those individuals to be separated while their eligibility is reviewed, and U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said he would issue a ruling Wednesday on the administration's request. "I think this case is really on the forefront of the administration's battle to fight for election integrity," Essayli said during a news conference Tuesday. "We wanna stop illegal voting. We don't wanna chase it later," he added. When asked about Seabright's ruling during the news conference, Essayli gave reporters a brief response. articles.title: Trump says he ‘made the mistake’ of ‘studying’ GOP senator’s ‘anatomy’
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday quipped that he made “the mistake” of “studying” Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) “anatomy,” after his remarks about the senator’s backside made headlines last week. “So I’m studying him, and I made the mistake of saying that I started off by studying his a–,” Trump told supporters during a rally in Lubbock,…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday quipped that he made “the mistake” of “studying” Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) “anatomy,” after his remarks about the senator’s backside made headlines last week.

“So I’m studying him, and I made the mistake of saying that I started off by studying his a–,” Trump told supporters during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, for Senate candidate Ken Paxton (R). “I just want to say. And then I looked at his feet and they were massive. Then I looked at his hand. ‘See these hands,’ he said.”

The president added that Husted’s hands were “fine” but that his fingers were “like sausages” and that his own hand hurt from shaking the senator’s.

“It was like hitting steel,” he continued, with rally attendees laughing. “But I made the mistake of studying his anatomy and explaining it to the audience, and the audience loved it.”

He acknowledged the press around his remarks, saying the “fake news” media wanted to know what Trump was doing “talking about a man’s anatomy.”

“After that, it was to see where the power came from, because he was a violent tackler,” Trump said, referring to Husted’s time as a defensive back for the Flyers at the University of Dayton.

The president has made several remarks about the Ohio Republican’s build in recent weeks, saying at a rally in North Carolina last week that he looked at Husted and said, “His a‑‑ is like, it’s like a pile of muscle.”

Husted leaned into the praise Tuesday, joking to supporters at a campaign event that he “was in the weight room” in anticipation of Trump’s return to the Buckeye State on Wednesday.

“I don’t want to let him down,” the senator added.

Trump has long remarked on people’s appearances. He has joked at rallies, White House events and elsewhere that his comments on women’s appearances could have him “canceled.” But the notes about men’s physiques have raised the eyebrows of commentators on both sides of the political spectrum.

Husted is locked in a tight race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who lost to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) in 2024.

The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ predicted on Tuesday that Brown has a 56-percent probability of defeating Husted in the Nov. 3 election.

The president has been on a campaign blitz to stir up GOP support in red states in the final week before the November midterm elections, looking to ensure that congressional Republicans maintain their hold on Capitol Hill. Democrats are favored to win back control of the House next week, with a narrow path to victory in reclaiming the Senate.

articles.title: Spurned by MAGA attacks, Arab-American voters defect to Democrats
articles.summary: The leftward shift of America’s Arab voters is undeniable, and almost all of it is driven by Republicans’ overt hostility.
articles.body:
This year’s midterm election cycle has been more grueling than most, and Republicans seem to be committed to making sure it doesn’t end without our national discourse hitting a new low. The disgraceful wave of anti-Arab and anti-Islamic rhetoric spewing out of MAGA officials in the campaign’s closing weeks should be cause for condemnation and moral reflection.

Given the sorry state of today’s Republican Party , we shouldn’t expect either.

MAGA’s Islamophobic hysteria is driven in one part by the national rise of Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed (D), and in another by the right’s open hostility to anyone they mistake for an immigrant . But Republicans’ anti-Arab screeching has now reached such a fever pitch that their attacks no longer make sense even as coherent thoughts. Is it any surprise that Arab-American voters are now fleeing the Republican Party in droves?

Republicans provide daily evidence for why many Arab Americans who supported President Trump in 2024 are now defecting to the Democratic Party . After all, it’s tough to claim your movement welcomes Arab-American votes when Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. can open a Michigan campaign event with the insane claim that “there’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize … they don’t produce literature.”

It wouldn’t kill Kennedy to read a book. He might even choose a work by the Syrian poet Ali Ahmad Said Esber, who writes under the pen name Adonis, or a work of fiction by Libyan novelist Ibrahim al-Koni, both of whom are considered leading contenders for this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature . Or Kennedy might consider diving into the sciences with Dr. Omar Yaghi, the Jordanian chemist who won last year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry . But Kennedy clearly prefers the sound of his own voice, even if he doesn’t know what he’s talking about.

Trump is also no stranger to bashing Arab Americans — even those who supported him in 2024. In the last few weeks alone, Trump has accused El-Sayed of being a “jihadist” and a “terrorist,” suggested he “ go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate ,” and dismissively referred to El-Sayed as “ Mohammed .” Trump’s comments have been so extreme his former 2024 Michigan outreach co-lead Bishara Bahbah publicly condemned him for crossing a “red line.”

“Any attack based on a person’s religion is not acceptable,” Bahbah told The Associated Press. “Abdul El-Sayed was born and raised in the United States. He’s as American as they come.”

Arab Americans and Muslims don’t even need to represent a large share of a state’s population to qualify for MAGA’s targeted hatred. In Alabama, where Muslims represent only about 0.5 percent of the population , Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) recently singled them out as “the enemy inside the gates” in what the Alabama Reflector calls his “anti-Muslim crusade.”

In Texas, where Muslims account for just 1 percent of residents , Gov. Greg Abbott (R) has ramped up attacks on the Muslim community in Plano over a planned Islamic community center that he claims will bring “sharia courts” to the Lone Star State, whatever that means.

Trump’s MAGA movement returned Arab-American voters’ loyalty with a heaping helping of vitriol and hatred. Now it’s those voters’ turn to have their say. A new Washington Post-Schar School poll published this month found that Arab Americans are taking MAGA venom at face value and moving away from a party that many conservative Arabs embraced just two years ago.

The leftward shift of America’s Arab voters is undeniable, and almost all of it is driven by Republicans’ overt hostility. In 2024, roughly 50 percent of Arab Americans supported Democratic candidates for Congress. After a year of being called terrorists and invaders by Trump and his allies, that number has climbed to nearly 60 percent.

A quarter of Arab Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 now say they plan to switch their vote and support Democrats this year, and a supermajority — 60 percent — say Trump is unfriendly to the Arab American community . Michigan alone is home to more than 200,000 registered Arab-American voters . In a race where Rep. Mike Rogers (R) is trailing El-Sayed by up to 6 points , those spurned Arab-American votes would have come in handy. Instead, Rogers and the Republicans chose to lob racist insults at them.

Republicans couldn’t be clearer that their party rejects the very idea that an Arab American can be an American at all. For the 3.7 million Arab Americans who are looking for a political home, the Democratic Party is happy to welcome you.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: South Carolina Senate race deadlocked: Survey
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and Democratic Senate hopeful Annie Andrews are deadlocked in the Palmetto State race with less than a week before Election Day, according to a new survey. The New York Times/Siena University poll, released Wednesday, shows both candidates with 48 percent support among likely voters in South Carolina — which has not…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and Democratic Senate hopeful Annie Andrews are deadlocked in the Palmetto State race with less than a week before Election Day, according to a new survey.

The New York Times/Siena University poll , released Wednesday, shows both candidates with 48 percent support among likely voters in South Carolina — which has not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber of Congress since 1998.

Among those surveyed, 73 percent said they were “almost certain” or at least somewhat likely to vote next Tuesday. Another 22 percent said they voted early. Meanwhile, 3 percent said they were less likely or not at all likely to cast a ballot, while 2 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

When asked if they were more likely to back a Democrat or Republican if the election were held today, 43 percent of respondents said Democrat while 51 percent said the GOP candidate, the survey found. The remaining 6 percent said they would choose another candidate or were unsure.

In recent weeks, Republicans have increased their spending to more than $20 million to back Graham in the high-stakes race to succeed her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R), after his sudden death , according to ad tracking firm AdImpact.

The incumbent, who was appointed to finish her brother’s term, has struggled to raise money throughout the campaign, and her support has come mainly from outside Republicans. Federal Election Commission filings show Darline Graham raised just $1.2 million as of Oct. 14, compared with Andrews’s $23.8 million.

President Trump has visited the state to boost support, most recently last week, and the Republican National Committee announced the president will return to the state on Thursday, just a few days ahead of the midterms.

Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), who ran against Graham in the special primary, said last week that while he would keep his promise to vote for Graham, his family would not be supporting her.

“I would not do an event with her, and I made that pretty clear,” Norman said during a radio interview. “When I conceded the race, I called her and congratulated her, but that’s the only time I’ve spoken with her.”

Democrats have been burned before in South Carolina, namely in the 2020 Senate race, where polls suggested a close contest between Lindsey Graham and former Democratic National Committee Chair Jaime Harrison (D). Harrison went on to lose by 10 points.

The close race is just one battle the GOP is fighting as it struggles to maintain its Senate majority.

According to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, the likeliest flips for Democrats in the Senate are North Carolina, Alaska, Texas and Ohio — amounting to the four seats they need to take back control of the chamber.

The party also has a greater than 40 percent chance in Iowa and Maine, and a greater than 30 percent chance in South Carolina and Kansas. DDHQ gives Darline Graham a 67 percent chance to win.

The Times/Siena poll was conducted Oct. 19-26 among 707 voters in South Carolina. The margin of error is 4.3 percentage points.

articles.body:
Democrat Peggy Flanagan is leading in the Minnesota Senate race against GOP competitor Michele Tafoya, according to a new poll.

In The New York Times/Siena University poll , 54 percent of respondents said they were more likely to cast their ballot for Flanagan if Election Day were that day, while 40 percent said the same for Tafoya. Less than half a percent chose another candidate, and 5 percent were unsure of their choice or gave no answer.

The double-digit gap between Flanagan and Tafoya is notable, as the Minnesota lieutenant governor was recently holding a slim lead over the former NFL reporter. And nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted the race toward the Republicans, from “likely” to “lean” Democrat, just a short time ago.

In a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Flanagan was leading Tafoya 47.4 percent to 43.8 percent on Wednesday morning .

The current political environment in the 2026 election cycle is appearing to favor Democrats, due to factors including the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living.

Amid the war in Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed, driving up energy prices. In Minnesota, the average price for a gallon of regular gas in the state on Wednesday morning was about $4.17, up from about $2.90 at the same time last year, according to AAA.

In the Times/Siena Minnesota poll, 35 percent of respondents said they “strongly approve” or “somewhat approve” of Trump’s job performance, while 62 percent said they “somewhat disapprove” or “strongly disapprove” of how the president is handling his job. Three percent were unsure about Trump’s job performance or did not respond.

The Times/Siena poll took place from Oct. 19-26, featuring 752 Minnesota voters and 4.1 percentage points as its margin of sampling error.

articles.title: Why relying on prediction markets in the elections may not be a safe bet
articles.summary: Will pollsters or the prediction markets provide the most accurate forecasts in the midterms?
articles.body:
The U.S. midterm elections are almost here.

Pollsters have been busy asking voters whether they are likely to vote and who they plan to vote for. This data indicates that there are several close races in the House, with Democrats holding a clear edge . Many Senate races are competitive in what have been traditional Republican strongholds like Texas and Alaska . Prediction markets have also entered the midterm prediction arena.

A question that candidates and voters may be asking is: Will pollsters or the prediction markets provide the most accurate forecasts? To assess this question requires a deep dive into both approaches.

Polling has evolved over time , yet its basic premise remains the same: sampling a group of people from which a prediction about an election outcome can be drawn. A sample of 1,000 people typically results in a plus or minus three-point margin of error . This means that in close races, like one where candidate A is polling at 49 percent, Candidate B is polling at 47 percent, and 4 percent are undecided, the margin of error dampens the value of polls as a predictive tool. There are many such races in this election cycle .

Prediction markets take an entirely different approach. People trade contracts based on a yes/no question. The balance between yes/no bets determines the price of contracts and the effective odds of winning. Prediction market contracts are priced between $0 and $1, which reflects the market’s estimate of a candidate’s probability of winning. For example, if a contract trades at 60 cents, the market assigns that candidate a 60 percent chance of victory. Note that prediction markets do not provide a margin of error for their forecast.

Looking back, prediction markets were assessed to be more predictive than polls for the 2024 presidential election. One possible explanation is that odds are set by people placing bets on who they believe will win. This contrasts with polls, where people are sampled by pollsters and asked questions about candidate preferences. This means that voters who place a bet are self-selected hoping to win money, while voters have no real choice on whether they are sampled by pollsters.

The bigger issue is whether people who engage with prediction markets are representative of the people who will vote. This then begs the question: Is money being wagered based on who bettors believe will win or who they want to win?

Given that anyone with access to a prediction market platform can place bets on the election, barring state restrictions , while only U.S. citizens are eligible to vote, there is no reason why prediction markets should serve as a reliable prediction tool. Moreover, the objective for bettors is to win money. To improve their odds, they are likely to assess all news information available, including polls. This means that polls inform prediction market odds, adding some dependency in their forecasts. Polls are also snapshots in time, while prediction markets dynamically update odds in real time as money flows to each candidate.

Americans are generally opposed to betting on elections; recent polls indicate that more Democrats than Republicans oppose election betting (69 percent versus 61 percent). Similarly, more Republicans than Democrats support election betting (16 percent versus 12 percent). Other betting demographics, like the high number of younger males, may further obfuscate the predictive value of prediction market odds. If Republican bias translates into bets being placed , this may give Republican candidates an edge in prediction markets that may not translate into the election outcomes, though arbitrage and market efficiencies will in theory correct for this.

Polling is a tried-and-true process for election prediction, while modern prediction markets are a modern phenomenon that has grown out of the digital economy. What will likely challenge both approaches in this year’s midterms is the large number of races with candidates polling well within the margin of error. Contradictory forecasts between polls and prediction markets are representative of true toss-ups.

Like every election, voter turnout matters. There is no way to determine this until after the election is complete. Factors like inclement weather on Election Day or an unexpected personal emergency can derail the best laid plans to vote.

If the demographics of people that show up to vote are not captured in polls, the polls are likely to provide misleading information. If the demographics of people placing bets in prediction markets do not represent how voters will act based on the amount of money wagered that set contract prices, they too will not offer much predictive value.

After the elections, the results will be reported and with 20-20 hindsight, both pollsters and prediction markets will claim their share of victories and explain away missteps. Yet the stakes are radically different. Future polling errors can be addressed by changing how polls are conducted. Prediction markets are a business platform where accuracy drives attention and revenue.

Of course, the true winners aren’t those who placed bets or pollsters conducting surveys, but rather, the voters who take the time to make their voices heard. They provide the data that matters most.

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. He applies his expertise in data-driven risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy.

articles.body:
Andrew Yang, the co-founder of the Forward Party who ran for Oval Office in 2020, said speculations about actor Matthew McConaughey running for office in 2028 have intensified.

“Well, I wouldn’t be alone. I’ll tell you that. I mean, the speculation has officially been stoked,” Yang told NewsNation’s Blake Burman, when asked if he would want to see McConaughey launch a bid.

The “Interstellar” star posted a video to social media earlier this month pressing voters to think more about independent candidates. He said supporting independents could bring lawmakers “back to the middle, where most American values live.”

Yang, who appeared on “The Hill” late Tuesday, said, “You don’t put out that kind of video if you’re not thinking about it.”

In his video, McConaughey added that he is endorsing two things: “Fairness and reality.”

“The No. 1 political identity in America today is not Republican. It is not Democrat. It is independent,” McConaughey said.

“So independents belong in the fight — not as a protest, not as a spoiler — but as a real and potential winner, on the ballot and considered seriously by us,” he continued.

A 2025 Gallup poll showed that 45 percent of U.S. adults identified with independent politics, while 27 percent identified as Democrats and another 27 percent identified as Republicans. The poll also indicated a higher percentage of Generation Z adults and millennials identified as political independents.

McConaughey’s independent agenda was supported by Texas’s Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico, who told TMZ DC that if the actor feels strongly about it, he should step up and run for office.

“I think he’d be a great candidate,” Talarico added.

When asked why he is running for Congress, the Democrat said it is “because of this two-party system, it’s near impossible to be able to get elected as an independent candidate.”

articles.title: Rename a real issue: America’s determinants of health
articles.summary: Over the past few years, politics has increasingly shaped these determinants, often in not so favorable ways.
articles.body:
The Gulf of Mexico has been renamed the Gulf of America , yet remains salty. Lake Ontario has been called Lake America , yet its winds still whip in the fall.

What has not been renamed, and needs to be, is the term “ social determinant of health .” It refers to the environmental, educational, economic and healthcare factors that have long been recognized as shaping our well-being and susceptibility to illness. The phrase has been part of the academic and public health lexicon for decades but means little to the public.

We recognize that the individual and collective decisions about our lifestyles — from the food we eat, to the education and healthcare we receive, to where and how we live — are determinants of our health. Over the last few years, politics has increasingly shaped these determinants, often in not so favorable ways.

Renaming these factors as “America’s determinants of health” can crystallize the notion that we have a critical role in the decisions that influence our health, especially during elections.

In America, health determinants begin during pregnancy, as healthcare, nutrition and housing influence pregnancy outcomes . Lack of healthcare access and inadequate nutrition are tied to maternal death and higher rates of premature births. Compared to other industrialized countries, the U.S. is among the worst when it comes to maternal mortality and premature birth rates.

In part, a determinant that is now shaping pregnancy and women’s health outcomes in the U.S. are anti-abortion policies, which are causing obstetricians to leave red states and resulting in healthcare deserts for pregnant women.

Early childhood factors also shape children’s and adults’ long-term health, including education, housing, diet and access to healthcare and vaccines. Health professionals call negative outcomes associated with those factors “ adverse childhood experiences ,” and they are tied to increased cardiovascular disease in adulthood.

As rates of vaccination fall because current federal leadership undermines immunization policies, we also now see the resurgence of vaccine-preventable illnesses that are blistering communities. Vaccine-related determinants of health extend far beyond childhood, as those administered in infancy confer lifelong protection against diseases that can affect tens of thousands of Americans, such as hepatitis B .

The mental and behavioral health of children, recognized as a national crisis , is affected by societal and economic factors. Contributing dynamics include social media, declining interpersonal interactions and inadequate pediatric mental health services. Despite recognizing the perils and impact of these determinants, it is surprising that America’s elected officials have not enacted federal laws regulating online media , while other countries have.

An incredible success story in public health has been efforts to stop tobacco use , which is a major contributor to cardiac and pulmonary disease and premature death. Yet whereas tobacco can be a personal choice, we do not have a choice in the air we breathe or the water we drink. Air and water pollution contribute to adverse health effects such as asthma and increased cancer risk, in those young and old. Yet, federal standards to reduce air and water pollution are being rolled back and will predictably harm health.

Our country has long recognized the consequences of poverty and hunger, along with the inability to afford food and healthcare. Thus, federal programs, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, help keep people fed. Medicaid , which 20 percent of Americans use, and Medicare , in which more than 90 percent of people older than 65 are enrolled, were created to support healthcare access.

However, with the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, more than $900 billion in Medicaid funding will be cut over the next 10 years, along with about $200 billion from SNAP. Americans who lose their healthcare and food assistance programs will face the consequences of these budget cuts.

These budget reductions disproportionately hurt rural America . In response, $50 billion has been allocated to the Rural Health Transformation Program , which focuses on chronic disease prevention by addressing social determinants of health. Yet, this funding will not alleviate the budget impact of H.R.1 , which could cause more than 20 percent of rural hospitals to close , a determinant of health in rural areas.

We recognize that the conditions we live in, the support our government provides and the public health and healthcare policies we enact come from us and those we elect. Americans shape their health determinants through policies and laws.

These are social determinants of health. Yet “social” is a word that can be seen by some as politically polarizing, and “social determinants” does not reflect the role of government in these factors.

Renaming great bodies of water does not change what they are. But reframing the idea that society and policy affect our health, and that the people we elect and the laws they pass can influence it, can. It shows that Americans have a role in controlling what determines their health.

Scott Rivkees, MD, is a pediatrician. He is the former state surgeon general and secretary of Health of Florida.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) referred to his fellow Republican senator, Sen. Bernie Moreno (Ohio), as “eye candy,” comments that come after President Trump complimented the physique of the other Ohio senator, Sen. Jon Husted (R).

“I know that Husted gets a ton of attention, but I think Bernie’s kind of eye candy too. I don’t know if — if you guys got, you both got the — they both got it going on when it comes to that,” Thune noted at a local Republican event in Ohio on Tuesday.

Thune’s comments follow Trump complimenting the backside of Husted, something he has done multiple times on the campaign trail as Election Day nears.

“I looked at his a‑‑, and then I looked at his legs, and my — I said, ‘His a‑‑ is like, it’s like a pile of muscle.’ Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big,’” Trump said during a rally in North Carolina last week, talking about Husted, who is locked in a tight race with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio).

“Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” the president added.

On Tuesday , Trump quipped that he had made “the mistake” of “studying” Husted’s “anatomy,” after the president’s remarks about Husted’s backside were in the national spotlight last week.

“So I’m studying him, and I made the mistake of saying that I started off by studying his a–,” Trump told supporters while at a Texas rally. “I just want to say. And then I looked at his feet and they were massive. Then I looked at his hand. ‘See these hands,’ he said.”

articles.title: 47 states allow early voting for all — what about the other three?
articles.summary: Some will say early voting is a convenience, not a right. I would answer this way: The right to vote is only as strong as the ability to exercise it.
articles.body:
This week I will walk into my polling place in Connecticut and cast my ballot early. Not because I am in a hurry, but because I will be out of the country on Election Day, and my state has made room for me to be heard anyway.

That is what democracy looks like when it expands. It meets people where they are.

Forty-seven states and the District of Columbia now let every voter cast a ballot early, no excuse required. Three do not: Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire.

I ask you to sit with that list for a moment.

The framers left the “Times, Places and Manner” of elections to the states. Nearly two and a half centuries later, that design still means your access to the ballot depends on where you live.

New Hampshire proudly holds the first presidential primary in the nation. Every four years, the country turns its eyes to the Granite State to begin choosing a president. Yet the state that goes first in picking our leaders is among the last to let every voter cast a ballot early. First in line for the cameras. Last in line for the voters.

On June 2, the Supreme Court voted six to three to let Alabama use its 2023 congressional map in next month’s election. A lower federal court had found that map discriminated against Black voters, by eliminating one of the state’s two majority-Black congressional districts . The ruling followed the court’s decision this spring in Louisiana v. Callais , which narrowed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, the very tool Americans have relied on for decades to challenge maps that dilute the power of Black voters.

The late Congressman John Lewis, who in 1965 was beaten in Selma, Ala. , fighting for the right to vote, once said , “The vote is precious. It is almost sacred. It is the most powerful non-violent tool we have in a democracy.”

Mississippi, too, is feeling the fallout. In 2025, a federal court ordered the state to redraw its legislative maps to give Black voters a fair chance to elect candidates of their choice. Now, after Callais , those hard-won districts are back in question, and state leaders are weighing whether to redraw them again before the 2027 elections.

So here is the pattern. In two of the three states that refuse early voting to all their citizens, the fight over who gets fair representation is fiercest. Fewer days to vote. Fewer districts where Black voters can elect a candidate of their choice. That is not an expansion of democracy. It is a contraction.

In 1964, Fannie Lou Hamer , a sharecropper from Mississippi who had been beaten by police the year after attending a voter registration workshop, told the nation she was “ sick and tired of being sick and tired. ” Sixty-two years later, in her own state, voters still cannot walk in early and cast a ballot without an excuse.

Some will say early voting is a convenience, not a right. I would answer this way: The right to vote is only as strong as the ability to exercise it. A single Tuesday does not work for the nurse on a double shift, the caregiver who cannot leave a parent alone, the soldier, the shift worker, or the woman who will be on the other side of the ocean on Election Day. Early voting does not change who is eligible. It changes who is able.

And Americans are using it. More than 18 million ballots have already been cast early, by mail or in person, and the count grows every day. In Louisiana, where Callais began, Black early turnout is its highest in recent history . In Alabama and Mississippi, there is no early vote to count. Their voters are still waiting for Tuesday.

The ballot is the door. Our job is to keep it open and open it wider.

Forty-seven states have chosen to trust their voters with more time. The remaining three should join them. In America’s 250th year, the question is not whether the ballot box is open. It is for whom, and for how long.

The midterms are less than a week away. If your state offers early voting, use it. If it does not, demand answers from your leaders.

When I board my flight, my ballot will already be cast. I will carry a simple belief with me: In a democracy, the door to the ballot box should never be narrower than the people it was built for.

Yvonne Renée Davis, MS, MA, PC, is founder, president and CEO of DAVISIntelligence , a strategic communications and crisis advisory firm. A former presidential appointee under President George W. Bush and U.S. Department of State communications trainer, she has worked across 68 countries and three presidential administrations.

articles.title: Former RNC chair: Democrats will ‘probably’ take House control
articles.summary: Former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Ronna McDaniel signaled Tuesday that Democrats were likely to regain control of the House with a week to go before the midterm elections. “I think the House, you know with three seats that the Dems need to pick up, is probably going to go to the Democrats,” she told…
articles.body:
Former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Ronna McDaniel signaled Tuesday that Democrats were likely to regain control of the House with a week to go before the midterm elections .

“I think the House, you know with three seats that the Dems need to pick up, is probably going to go to the Democrats,” she told CBS News’s Major Garrett. “And right now, all eyes are on the Senate, but certainly the map has expanded and Democrats are feeling bullish.”

The Democratic Party has around an 80 percent chance of retaking control of the lower chamber of Congress, according to Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) latest projection. Democrats have a narrower advantage in the Senate, with DDHQ placing the party’s odds of regaining the majority in the upper chamber at around 57 percent.

McDaniel, who oversaw the RNC from 2017 to 2024, also pointed to President Trump’s recent travel to red states like Kansas, South Carolina, Mississippi and Texas as indications of electoral trouble for Republicans this midterm cycle .

“I know for a fact, you’re not in these states unless there’s a data point that’s driving him to spend time in those states,” she continued. “How many times has he been to Texas? I mean, we shouldn’t be spending $200 million or $300 million in Texas to defend a Senate candidate, so there’s a lot at stake.”

Trump made his fourth visit to the Lone Star State in the past two months on Tuesday for two rallies with the GOP’s Senate nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, in Corpus Christi and Lubbock.

The president’s political PAC, MAGA Inc., has donated millions to support the attorney general in his race against state Rep. James Talarico (D). The Democrat has also raised a significant amount of money throughout his campaign, reporting nearly $10 million in cash on hand in Federal Election Commission filings earlier this month.

Talarico has performed well in polling among likely voters in the state, raising concerns among Republicans that he could be the first Democratic candidate to win a U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988.

During the president’s rallies in Texas on Tuesday, Trump criticized the candidate for his stance on issues like immigration and energy and used his preferred nickname for the Democrat, “Talafreako.”

Talarico brushed off the attacks in a Lubbock rally held the same day .

“That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room,” he told a crowd of supporters before declaring the state was “ready for change.”

articles.title: Top federal prosecutor in LA not legally serving, judge rules
articles.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, is unlawfully serving as the top prosecutor in Los Angeles. U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright wrote in his order that the former California State Assembly member “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, is unlawfully serving as the top prosecutor in Los Angeles.

U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright wrote in his order that the former California State Assembly member “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney” and is “disqualified from participating in or supervising” cases.

Seabright, who was appointed by former President George W. Bush, also wrote that the Department of Justice (DOJ) unlawfully delegated powers that have kept Essayli in the role after the 120-day legal limit for acting U.S. attorneys. The order will go into effect after the court rules on the government’s motion for a stay pending appeal.

Essayli learned about Seabright’s ruling in the Los Angeles Times and told the outlet that his office expected it.

“Just so there’s no confusion, today’s order is stayed and has no immediate effect,” he wrote on the social platform X . “I remain First Assistant U.S. Attorney and continue running the office. The Supreme Court will ultimately decide this matter.”

The Trump administration appointed Essayli last year to serve in an acting capacity, with former Attorney General Pam Bondi appointing him to be the first assistant U.S. attorney before the 120-day limit hit.

Seabright blocked Essayli from overseeing criminal cases after declaring that the prosecutor was in the role longer than legally allowed in October 2025.

He wrote on Tuesday that his appointment was “identical” to that of the Trump administration’s appointee for U.S. attorney in Nevada, Sigal Chattah, who the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals found to be unlawfully appointed .

The defense attorney who challenged Essayli’s authority in August, H. Dean Steward, called Seabright’s ruling “a victory for the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution.”

“The Trump administration ignored the laws governing the appointment of U.S. Attorneys and got caught in Los Angeles,” Steward told the Times. “Trump and his Department of Justice violated the law again and again in an effort to install minions as chief federal prosecutors.”

Essayli has overseen the DOJ’s legal fight with California officials over 20,000 noncitizens allegedly on state voter rolls. The prosecutor said the department’s request to California counties to identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls was “simple” and said election officials not complying with the DOJ will be held accountable.

The Trump administration has sought to install prosecutors across the country without confirmation in the Senate, but this has opened up more legal battles.

An appeals court ruled in December that the administration’s choice to be New Jersey’s top prosecutor, Alina Habba, was unlawfully appointed. Another federal judge found in January that Lindsey Halligan “ may not serve ” as U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia because of an unlawful appointment.

articles.title: Alaska’s GOP-led government asks court to block DOJ Senate race certification lawsuit
articles.summary: Alaska’s GOP-led government is urging a federal court to dismiss the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) lawsuit seeking to bar the state from certifying its midterm election results, according to a Monday court filing. The DOJ lawsuit, filed last week, claimed the presence of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could…
articles.body:
Alaska’s GOP-led government is urging a federal court to dismiss the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) lawsuit seeking to bar the state from certifying its midterm election results, according to a Monday court filing.

The DOJ lawsuit , filed last week , claimed the presence of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could give Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola an unfair advantage in the upcoming election.

In a motion to dismiss , attorneys representing Alaska and the other defendants named in the lawsuit said the state’s elections division “has taken significant steps to distinguish them on the ballot so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which.”

The state’s filing also noted “the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate,” adding “the complaint has no legal basis.”

The Justice Department’s lawsuit, which President Trump said he directed to be filed , claimed the other Dan Sullivan — Republican Daniel J. Sullivan — entered the Senate race “with the intention of misleading” the incumbent senator’s supporters.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” the DOJ’s filing read.

Following the lawsuit, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department is not trying to stop the certification of Alaska’s election but is instead seeking “to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead.”

A copy of the designed ballot attached to the state’s filing shows the word “incumbent” next to the GOP senator’s name, along with his party affiliation. It does not mention the other Sullivan’s registered Republican status.

It also noted the two candidates’ middle initials to differentiate them; the incumbent senator is listed as “Sullivan, Dan S.” while the other candidate is labeled “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”

Lawyers for Peltola’s campaign also asked the court to dismiss the DOJ lawsuit , calling it “wholly baseless.” Last week, nonprofit watchdog group Common Cause, represented by attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union, also filed a motion to intervene in the legal challenge.

On Monday, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ordered to expedite the consideration of the case , giving the federal government until 5 p.m. Tuesday to respond to both Peltola’s and Common Cause’s motions.
