articles.title: Put AI to work on America’s electric bill
articles.summary: Software can fix a lot of this — if lawmakers let it.
articles.body:
Electric bills are rising for too many American families. The average household is paying about 18 cents per kilowatt-hour this year . That’s up roughly 10 percent in just two years. In fact, from 2021 to 2025, residential electricity prices climbed nearly 30 percent , far outpacing the rate of inflation .

Like all kitchen table issues, those increased costs have a real-life impact, as every dollar spent on electric bills is one less available to put food on the table, fuel in the car or in the coming weeks, put Christmas presents under the tree.

And while there are obvious connections between rising costs like gasoline and the conflict in Iran , consumers are reasonably left wondering: What’s driving up my household electric bill? And how can we bring that cost back down?

A bill recently introduced in the Senate represents a crucial step toward doing just that by upgrading our existing power lines and using advanced computing to connect new generators to the grid faster than ever. And less than a week before Election Day, this legislation features something hard to find at this time of year: bipartisan consensus.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 was introduced late last month by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) — the chairs and ranking members, respectively, of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

It’s the most serious attempt at federal permitting reform in decades, tackling some of the key problems with federal agencies’ approaches to reviewing and approving projects to build and upgrade infrastructure, including the electrical grid.

As multiple studies have found, these permitting problems often add exorbitant costs and cause lengthy, unnecessary delays to energy projects. That ultimately reduces the amount of electricity available, which then drives up the price that consumers are forced to pay.

Consider how difficult it is to build new power lines to deliver electricity. Last year, only about 400 miles of new high-capacity transmission lines were finished across the country. That’s a far cry from the nearly 5,000 miles per year of additional capacity that industry analysts estimate we need to keep up with demand.

While that bottleneck deserves a solution, the act also paves the way for an easier fix: reconductoring, or replacing older wires on existing power lines with advanced ones that carry more electricity on the same route. Industry studies show that advanced conductors can effectively double capacity on most existing lines at less than half the cost per mile and a fraction of the time it would take to build new ones.

The Senate proposal would allow upgrades within existing power line corridors to skip full environmental and historic reviews. It would also have federal regulators require the utilities they oversee to use advanced grid technologies, including the best available wires, when they build or upgrade lines.

In energy policy, unlike with electricity, it is best to follow the path of least resistance. That should also be true for hooking up new energy sources to the grid.

Currently, before a new power plant can connect, engineers must study whether the grid can handle that additional power safely and determine what upgrades it needs. But those studies, which are part of the interconnection process, have become a bottleneck. The average project that came online in 2025 took about five years from request to operation . A decade ago, it only took three. The result? Over 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting in line, more than the entire installed power plant fleet today.

Software can fix a lot of this, though — if lawmakers let it.

Midcontinent Independent System Operator, which manages much of the electric grid and wholesale energy market across the Midwest, recently took a study phase that required 686 days and reran it with automated study software. That rerun finished in 10 days , including setup and debugging, with similar estimates of upgrade costs.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would push the U.S. energy industry in that direction. It directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to start a rulemaking so grid operators share and use artificial intelligence, machine learning and automation to speed up study results. It also requires that grid data be available in forms automated studies can actually use.

Of course, even as the legislation encourages using artificial intelligence to help bring down Americans’ power bill, the act ensures that AI doesn’t simultaneously increase costs. Under the bill, data centers would pay the full cost of the transmission they require , and the federal Energy Information Administration would begin tracking how much electricity data centers use to ensure policymakers and voters alike have visibility into their impact on the grid.

None of this will shrink anyone’s bill overnight. But getting more out of the wires we have and clearing away avoidable delays for new power are credible ways to dramatically ease pressure on American families in the years ahead.

To achieve the prosperity every American wants, our country needs a lot of electricity. Under the Senate’s new proposal, we can unleash more of it at lower costs to households nationwide.

Taylor Barkley is the director of Federal Government Affairs and Policy Advisor at the Abundance Institute.

articles.title: Peltola denies NYT report her campaign recruited other Sullivan
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign and national Democrats are denying a new investigation from The New York Times reporting that they worked together to recruit candidates in an effort to pull votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska. The Times report, published Wednesday, cites twelve sources and references text messages and documents showing that…
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign and national Democrats are denying a new investigation from The New York Times reporting that they worked together to recruit candidates in an effort to pull votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska.

The Times report, published Wednesday, cites twelve sources and references text messages and documents showing that Peltola campaign aides, the campaign’s lawyers and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) staffers were involved in pushing other candidates, including Dan J. Sullivan, to run.

“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” the Peltola campaign said in a statement to The Times.

The DSCC also told The Hill in a statement it had “no involvement” in recruiting the other Sullivan. Peltola’s campaign did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The report comes just days after the Justice Department sued to block the Senate contest’s results from certification if the incumbent loses, citing the two Sullivans on the ballot.

The Peltola campaign has asked the judge to dismiss that case , prompting the judge to expedite the litigation.

Republicans, including the senator and President Trump, have long accused Democrats of recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.

Ballot “stacking” is a common practice, especially in Alaska’s unusual nonpartisan top-four voting system. Both parties have recruited fringe candidates this cycle and in previous years , hoping to siphon off votes.

According to The Times, the Peltola campaign’s effort to “stack” the ballot began in the summer of 2025, when DSCC aides connected the campaign to Democratic operatives who had experience with such maneuvers.

Those operatives, The Times’s sources claimed, coordinated with the campaign to recruit Dan J. Sullivan, who previously supported Peltola in elections, to run as a Republican. He recently changed his party affiliation from Republican to “undeclared.”

The operatives, per The Times, also attempted to recruit other candidates, meeting with an unconnected progressive candidate who made it on the primary ballot. This candidate dropped out of the race shortly after, the outlet reported.

Aides from the campaign and the DSCC, as well as a lawyer, also reportedly floated forming a “MAGA party” to challenge the Republican senator from the right.

The Senate race in Alaska is one of the most contested in the country as Democrats seek to win flip the upper chamber.

Peltola, who previously served in the House, is currently favored to win based on polls and other metrics, according to Decision Desk HQ.

articles.title: Harris advises Democrats against attempting to impeach Trump
articles.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday urged Democrats against making a third attempt to impeach President Trump if they win back the House after next week’s midterm elections. “I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you,” Harris told MeidasTouch’s Aaron Parnas in…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday urged Democrats against making a third attempt to impeach President Trump if they win back the House after next week’s midterm elections.

“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you,” Harris told MeidasTouch’s Aaron Parnas in an interview. “Just because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to put into accountability, need to be put into investigations.”

“And that’s where the time should be spent,” she added. “Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-around, and the votes aren’t there. “So, that’s how I feel. But also, I think after the election, we all have to just also agree that our attitude has to be to get stuff done.”

Harris said Democrats should be “uncompromising” and “not sit around, you know, being genteel about the relationships,” but maintain accountability when it comes to cuts to healthcare and oversight on the Iran war.

The former vice president was days into her new role in 2021 when Democratic lawmakers impeached Trump in connection with the Jan. 6 Capitol Hill attack. In February 2021, the Senate acquitted Trump in a 57-43 vote, with all Democrats voting “guilty,” joined by seven Republican senators, but falling short of the 67 votes needed to convict the then-former president.

Democrats have not ruled out making a third impeachment attempt if they win back the House next week, nor have they ruled out impeaching members of the administration like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“We’ve got to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution, and then let the chips fall where they may, in the best interests of the American people,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told ABC News last month when asked about pursuing another Trump impeachment.

Trump and Republican congressional leaders have insisted that Democrats will attempt to impeach the president next year.

“It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day — first or second day,” House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Tuesday in an interview with Scott Jennings, a pro-Trump pundit. “Remember, they’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress. And they’re raring to go.”

A third impeachment would be unprecedented, with Trump already holding the distinction of being the only U.S. president impeached twice. Efforts to impeach former President Andrew Johnson in 1868 and Bill Clinton in 1999 ended in acquittals, and former President Richard Nixon faced a likely impeachment before he resigned the presidency in 1974.

Democratic lawmakers first impeached Trump in late 2019, with Trump accused of requesting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to investigate then-former Vice President Biden and his family before launching his 2020 presidential campaign, eventually defeating Trump.

The Senate acquitted Trump in a 48-52 vote on abuse of power and 47-53 on obstruction in February 2020.

articles.title: Breast cancer prevention starts with knowing your risk
articles.summary: Rep. Julia Letlow introduced the Know Your Risk Act to direct the Department of Health and Human Services to create a universal breast cancer risk assessment tool.
articles.body:
My mother’s journey as a triple-negative breast cancer survivor showed me firsthand just how important it is to understand your own breast cancer risk.

A subsequent risk assessment revealed that I had a high probability of developing breast cancer, spurring me to take action and undergo a double mastectomy to reduce my future risk. While this was not a decision I made lightly, I welcomed the opportunity to take preventative action after learning about my high risk.

That experience reinforced my belief that every woman deserves the same opportunity to understand her risk and make informed decisions about her health. I believe such an outcome starts with creating a universal tool to assess an individual’s breast cancer risk.

Breast Cancer Awareness Month is a time to celebrate significant progress in reducing breast cancer deaths , while also acknowledging the challenges that remain. With more widely available screening and detection services, women increasingly have more opportunities to identify risks and address a potential diagnosis early.

However, there is still more work to do to combat a disease that many of us know all too well.

In addition to continuing to close gaps in care in places like rural Louisiana, we must reduce barriers that prevent women from understanding their likelihood of developing breast cancer. This includes making available a universal risk assessment.

Risk assessment tools are valuable resources that evaluate an individual’s likelihood of developing breast cancer based on factors such as family history, reproductive history and lifestyle. But the proliferation of these tools, each relying on different metrics, has often created confusion.

Many women also report a lack of awareness about the value of risk assessments, according to research from the National Institutes of Health . A clear, go-to assessment, combined with greater education about its value, would help more women better understand their risk and take appropriate action.

That is what my recently introduced Know Your Risk Act aims to accomplish. My bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services to create a universal tool that Americans can rely on, while expanding access to risk assessment services through the National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program.

The need for a more consistent approach is clear. There are currently dozens of breast cancer risk assessment tools on the market, with varying levels of accuracy and effectiveness. A more streamlined, evidence-based approach is needed.

For example, existing risk assessment tools are often used inconsistently in clinical settings. They are also available across multiple formats, including paper-based questionnaires and digital applications, and evaluate different populations in different ways.

A universal tool would provide women with clearer, more consistent access to information about their risk. It could also encourage more women at elevated risk to discuss preventative options with their doctors — decisions that could make a life-saving difference.

Early intervention played a crucial role in helping me understand my risk and guiding my decision to take preventative action. To ensure every woman has that same opportunity, our nation’s leading health agencies must work to ensure that no American is left in the dark about her breast cancer risk.

The National Institutes of Health’s newly established Women’s Health Division can play a key role in advancing research, as can emerging artificial intelligence tools. Women should also consult their doctors about mammograms and regular screenings to help identify potential concerns early.

Statistically, one in eight women will develop breast cancer in her lifetime, and early intervention can improve treatment outcomes and the odds of survival. Ensuring that every woman can access a reliable risk assessment is a crucial step toward better prevention and care. I will continue working to make that future a reality.

Rep. Julia Letlow represents Louisiana’s 5th District in the U.S. House of Representatives. She serves as vice chair of the House Appropriations subcommittee dedicated to healthcare issues.

It’s Wednesday, and we’re officially less than one week out from Election Day. Have you hit the polls yet?

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Julia Boehning, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and jboehning@thehill.com .

Legal battles are heating up as Election Day approaches. The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams dive deep into the lawsuits shaping the midterms and what’s next on “The Gavel.” Insiders can click here to join the live discussion and Q&A at 3 p.m. EDT.

Former President Obama heads to Atlanta on Wednesday afternoon to boost incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff’s (D-Ga.) reelection bid and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms , an appearance coming hot off his headline-making visit to Cleveland over the weekend.

While stumping for Democrats in Ohio, Obama spent much of his time at the podium roasting the Trump administration. One of his quips — that President Trump ‘s $900 million renovations to the White House looked “like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory” — really triggered the right.

Trump swipes back: The president responded to Obama’s jab while en route to his own rally in Mississippi on Monday — part of his late October midterm campaigning blitz.

Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews the Democrat didn’t understand “the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly” before slamming Obama as “a lousy president.”

Other administration voices weighed in on the spat, including multimillionaire Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , as The Hill’s Mira Bhakta covered earlier this week. While speaking outside a Cheesecake Factory, Bessent claimed he was a regular at the restaurant and slammed the design of the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.

Peach State push: The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), gives Ossoff an 86 percent chance of beating his GOP opponent, Rep. Mike Collins.

The race for governor is closer. According to DDHQ, Bottoms is “narrowly favored” to win the gubernatorial seat over Republican businessperson Rick Jackson .

Later Wednesday evening, Trump will return to Ohio for the third time this month — aiming to boost turnout for GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Sen. Jon Husted (R), who’s seeking reelection this November.

The president’s visit to Ohio comes four days after Obama’s. He’s set to stump in Chillicothe — a few hours south of Cleveland — at 7 p.m. EDT.

It’s Trump’s first visit to Ohio since Ramaswamy’s attack ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton ‘s estranged mother sparked a national firestorm. Husted said he wouldn’t have run the ad, but Trump and Vice President Vance jumped to Ramaswamy’s defense.

Husted hits the gym: The president said during a Tuesday rally in Lubbock, Texas, he “made the mistake” of studying Husted’s “anatomy” after previously saying, “His a‑‑ is like, it’s like a pile of muscle.”

Husted has leaned into the comments, quipping Tuesday he “was in the weight room” ahead of Trump’s visit. Senate Majority Leader John Thune got in on the fun during remarks in Ohio on Tuesday night.

The Federal Reserve will make its last interest rate decision ahead of midterms on Wednesday, with the expectation that it will remain steady despite persistent inflation.

According to the consumer price index, September’s inflation was listed at 3.7 percent, an increase from August’s 3.4 percent.

The Hill’s Max Rego wrote that “despite that data, multiple central bank officials — including Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and John Williams , the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — have recently said they will evaluate economic trends before backing another rate hike.”

Wait for December?: After Wednesday, the Fed will not meet again until Dec. 7-8 , when it could approve another interest rate hike.

According to the tool CME FedWatch, which forecasts Fed funds, traders said Tuesday there is a 92.8 percent chance rates will remain steady. It predicts a nearly 80 percent chance of a hike in December.

Ellen Meade , a former policy and communications adviser to the Fed, told The Hill not to “expect them to move this week.”

“I’m not expecting them to do anything other than maybe update in the statement their characterization of the economy,” Meade said.

Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in the state’s gubernatorial race.

“Our future is too important to be hamstrung by partisan divisions,” Murkowski said in a statement released by Kreiss-Tomkins’s campaign. “Jonathan understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”

The Alaska Republican has ripped the GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy , saying that his administration has “left federal money on the table.”

“I think in certain areas, where we have worked hard to put opportunities from the federal side, here, into the state, the state has failed with it,” Murkowski told Alaska News Source in an interview.

Trump’s bad side: Murkowski has been bashed by Trump for consistently crossing party lines, with the president calling her the “Republican’s Worst Senator” and a “DISGRACE to Alaska and our country.”

The senator previously endorsed Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola in her reelection run for House in 2024. In this year’s midterm cycle, Murkowski has endorsed Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan against Peltola.
